<reason>CON built a genuine fork (the field either records checkable sex or an uncheckable self-report) and then, unusually, made PRO's best rebuttal do CON's work: once PRO conceded the marker records no biology, no medical fact, and is not what officers actually match, CON turned that into "the letter is inert, so delete it rather than expand it," and offered deletion as an alternative that spares the mismatch for everyone (including androgynous people who are not nonbinary) without the state certifying belief. PRO answered pressure directly and well, cleanly dissolving the "second look" contradiction and giving a decent linkage answer via the surname analogy, and its "papers that match the presenter" frame was concrete and intuitive. But PRO's case against deletion rested largely on assertion ("maximal disruption," "coercion of 330 million," "inequality" for a uniform rule) and it never squarely answered why the state should print a self-declared category rather than drop a field it had just described as non-identifying. CON's win is narrow because of real execution costs: two clipped turns and repeated references to nonexistent [P2.x] IDs, plus an ad hoc "origin record" theory and an unanswered point about passports remaining binary under partial deletion.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 (A4.5–A4.6): seizing PRO's own A1 that identification runs "by photo, number, name and birthdate, not by matching sex letters" and arguing that if the letter is inert, deletion costs identification nothing and protects more people than X — PRO's "second look that resolves itself" reply was coherent but did not explain why X beats removing the field.</best_rebuttal>
